companyCaseStudy.title: How LinkedIn Scaled Kafka to 1+ Trillion Events/Day (~11.6M msg/s) — from Batch Lag to Real‑Time Streams
companyCaseStudy.summary: LinkedIn needed to move from brittle, batchy ETL pipelines to a real‑time backbone. They built Kafka and its ecosystem to handle over 1 trillion messages per day (≈11.6M msgs/sec average), cut end‑to‑end pipeline lag from minutes to seconds, and enabled dozens of real‑time applications.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
LinkedIn was ingesting and routing data for dozens of systems — activity feeds, metrics, search indexing, ads, alerts — and their batch pipelines couldn't keep up. The result: slow analytics, delayed feeds, fragile coupling between teams. The gamble: design a distributed log that can sustain *over 1 trillion messages per day* and serve both real‑time and offline consumers reliably.

## Problem
- Multiple point‑to‑point pipelines tied producers and consumers directly. Failures rippled across teams.
- Writers would overload downstream systems, causing backpressure and cascading failures.
- Batch jobs produced minutes-to-hours of lag; real‑time features were impossible.
- Storage and throughput at the scale LinkedIn needed required rethinking the IO model.

Numbers that mattered:
- Target ingest: over 1 trillion messages/day (~11.6M msgs/sec average)
- Want sub‑second to second consumer lag for many use cases
- Durable retention: keep event logs for minutes to days for replay and recovery

## Challenge
Design a system that:
- Scales horizontally to millions of messages per second
- Keeps writes fast and durable without random I/O penalty
- Lets many heterogeneous consumers read at their own pace
- Provides replication and availability across failures
- Is operationally manageable at LinkedIn’s scale

## Solution — Kafka's key ideas (what LinkedIn built)
- Append‑only partitioned logs: writes are sequential, append-only files (fast disk I/O).
- Partitioning: topics split into partitions so producers/consumers scale linearly.
- Batching + zero‑copy: large batches reduce per‑message overhead; OS page cache + sendfile/zero‑copy avoid extra copies.
- Replication & ISR: each partition has a leader and replicas; in‑sync replica (ISR) set ensures durability.
- Retention semantics: time/size retention and log compaction for use cases needing latest‑per‑key.
- ZooKeeper-based coordination (original architecture): leader election and metadata storage (later replaced by Kafka controllers).
- Stream processing integration: Samza (and later Kafka Streams) to process events in real time.

### Architecture (high level)
```mermaid
graph LR
  Producers[Producers (apps, sensors, services)] -->|Partition Key| KafkaBrokerCluster[Kafka Brokers]
  subgraph Kafka Cluster
    KafkaBrokerCluster --> ZK[ZooKeeper]
  end
  KafkaBrokerCluster --> ConsumersA[Consumers: Search Indexing]
  KafkaBrokerCluster --> ConsumersB[Consumers: Metrics/Monitoring]
  KafkaBrokerCluster --> ConsumersC[Consumers: Real‑time Feed]
  KafkaBrokerCluster --> HDFS[Hadoop/Offline ETL]
  ConsumersC --> Samza[Samza Stream Jobs]
```

## Concrete decisions and tuning LinkedIn used
- Use large segment files and tuned flush/segment sizes to amortize disk seeks.
- Rely on OS page cache: keep reads fast by working with the kernel cache, not custom caches.
- Tune producer batching and linger.ms so writes form big batches during bursts.
- Replication factor typically 2–3 for availability; careful monitoring of under‑replicated partitions.
- Monitor key metrics: bytes in/out, messages in per partition, ISR sizes, controller leader changes, GC pauses.
- Provide client libraries and strong compatibility guarantees so teams could adopt quickly.

## Results (real numbers and effects)
| Metric | Before | After (Kafka @ LinkedIn) |
|--------|--------:|-------------------------:|
| End‑to‑end pipeline lag | Minutes → Hours | Seconds → Sub‑second for many flows |
| Peak throughput | 100k–1M msgs/s (legacy pipelines) | Over 1 trillion msgs/day (~11.6M msgs/s average), peaks much higher |
| Operational decoupling | Tight point‑to‑point coupling | Many consumers read independently (fan‑out) |
| Feature velocity | Slow to add real‑time features | Rapid — many teams plugged into the log |

Real impacts:
- Enabled real‑time feed updates (lower latency for user visible activity).
- Simplified delivery: producers write once; 10s or 100s of consumers can independently subscribe.
- Supported both online (real‑time search, alerts) and offline (Hadoop ETL) consumers from the same durable log.

## Tradeoffs and lessons
- Complexity: introducing a distributed system with ZooKeeper-driven metadata added operational burden.
- Durability vs latency: replication increases durability but can increase write latency if you wait for ISR acknowledgements.
- Partitioning choices matter: hot keys (very skewed partitions) create hot brokers — choose keys and partition counts carefully.

## Visualization: simplified flow for a write and durable fan‑out
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Producer app] --> B[Batch & compress]
  B --> C[Partition leader broker]
  C --> D[Append to segment; fsync/replicate to ISR]
  D --> E[Consumer reads at offset X]
  E --> F[Real‑time service / Samza job]
```

## Why it mattered
By rethinking the storage and messaging model (append‑only, partitioned log), LinkedIn turned messaging into a durable, highly scalable backbone. This allowed the company to build real‑time applications that were previously impossible with batch pipelines and reduced coupling across teams.

## Final notes
Kafka has evolved (controller quorum replaced ZooKeeper in newer versions), but the core design principles from LinkedIn — sequential IO, partitioning, batching, replication — remain the foundation for modern event streaming at massive scale.
keyTakeaways: Design append‑only partitioned logs to convert random I/O into sequential writes — this unlocks multi‑million msgs/sec throughput (LinkedIn handled over 1 trillion messages/day).
Batching, zero‑copy I/O, and careful OS page‑cache usage are critical for high throughput and low CPU overhead.
Partitioning and replication are double‑edged: they enable scale and durability but require careful key design, monitoring of ISR, and operational practices.

concept.title: Sagas: How to Do Reliable Distributed Transactions Without 2PC
concept.summary: Distributed systems often need to update multiple services in one logical operation (e.g., place order, charge card, reserve inventory). Sagas give you a pragmatic, scalable way to achieve *eventual consistency* by sequencing local transactions and compensations instead of locking everything with 2PC.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters — the real problem

Imagine an e‑commerce checkout: you must charge the customer, reserve inventory, and create a shipment. These are owned by three different services. If charging succeeds but inventory reservation fails, how do you avoid money taken without the product being shipped? Traditional 2PC (two‑phase commit) is heavy, blocking, and brittle across microservices. Sagas solve this by turning a single logical transaction into a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions for failures.

**Analogy — Booking a trip**

Booking a trip often involves flight, hotel, and car rental. If the flight booking goes through but the hotel booking fails, you call the airline to cancel the flight — a *compensation* for the earlier action. That’s a saga.

---

## Two flavors of Sagas

- **Orchestration**: A central *orchestrator* tells each service what to do and, on failure, instructs compensations.
- **Choreography**: Services publish events and react to each other. Each service knows how to roll back its own action upon receiving a failure event.

### Mermaid sequence (Orchestration example)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Orchestrator
  participant Payment
  participant Inventory
  participant Shipping

  Orchestrator->>Payment: Charge(card)
  Payment-->>Orchestrator: Success
  Orchestrator->>Inventory: Reserve(item)
  Inventory--xOrchestrator: Failure
  Orchestrator->>Payment: Refund(chargeId)  
  Payment-->>Orchestrator: Refunded
  Orchestrator-->>Client: Failure (rolled back)
```

### Mermaid flowchart (Choreography example)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[OrderCreated Event] --> B[Payment Service]
  B -->|PaymentSucceeded| C[Inventory Service]
  C -->|InventoryReserved| D[Shipping Service]
  C -->|InventoryFailed| E[PaymentRefund]
  E --> F[OrderFailed]
```

---

## BEFORE vs AFTER: Monolith / 2PC vs Sagas

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| Two‑phase commit (2PC) | Strong consistency, ACID across services | Locks resources, high latency, brittle across networks | When absolute atomicity is required and services support transactions/coordination |
| Sagas (orchestration) | Scalable, non‑blocking, observable central flow | Eventual consistency, compensations required, complexity in orchestrator | Microservices with independent local transactions and requirement for availability |
| Sagas (choreography) | Highly decoupled, easy to scale, event driven | Harder to reason about system flow, debugging and monitoring harder | Event-driven systems with many small services and mature event infra |

---

## Simple orchestrator example (Node.js pseudocode)

```js
// Orchestrator: placeOrder
async function placeOrder(order) {
  const charge = await paymentService.charge(order.user, order.total)
  try {
    const reserve = await inventoryService.reserve(order.items)
    const shipment = await shippingService.createShipment(order)
    return { status: 'completed', shipment }
  } catch (err) {
    // Compensation: undo the charge
    await paymentService.refund(charge.id)
    return { status: 'failed', reason: err.message }
  }
}
```

## Choreography example (pseudo-event flow)

1. Order Service publishes `OrderCreated` event.
2. Payment Service consumes it, charges card, publishes `PaymentSucceeded` or `PaymentFailed`.
3. Inventory Service consumes `PaymentSucceeded`, tries to reserve items, publishes `InventoryReserved` or `InventoryFailed`.
4. On `InventoryFailed`, a service publishes `InventoryFailed` which triggers Payment Service to refund.

```text
OrderCreated -> PaymentService -> PaymentSucceeded -> InventoryService -> InventoryFailed -> PaymentService(refund)
```

---

## Practical concerns and common pitfalls

- **Compensating actions are not always perfect**: Compensation may not fully undo side effects (e.g., refunds take time). Design for eventual correctness.
- **Idempotency**: Every action and compensation must be idempotent. Retries and duplicate events are inevitable.
- **Ordering and concurrency**: Concurrent sagas touching the same business entity can race. Use optimistic concurrency tokens or application-level locks when necessary.
- **Long‑running transactions**: Sagas can span minutes or hours (e.g., human approval). Monitor and set clear timeouts and human remediation paths.
- **Observability**: Choreography can be hard to trace. Add correlation IDs, structured events, and end‑to‑end tracing to follow a saga.
- **Partial failure visibility**: Implement a dashboard for sagas stuck in compensating or pending states.
- **Complex compensations**: Some actions are irreversible (e.g., sending a physical package). Design workflows to avoid irreversible steps before guarantees are in place.

---

## When to choose Sagas

Choose sagas when you need high availability and your system can tolerate eventual consistency. Avoid sagas when you need strict immediate consistency across services (then consider centralized DB or tightly coupled transactional approaches), or where compensations are impossible.

---

## Quick checklist for implementing sagas

- Design each operation as a local transaction + compensation.
- Make all operations idempotent.
- Decide orchestration vs choreography based on complexity and team boundaries.
- Add correlation IDs and tracing for each saga instance.
- Implement timeouts, retries, and a human remediation path.

---

## Real example: Order processing (orchestration)

- Step 1: Orchestrator requests PaymentService. If success continue.
- Step 2: Orchestrator requests InventoryService to reserve stock. If fails -> orchestrator tells PaymentService to refund.
- Step 3: Orchestrator requests ShippingService to create shipment.

This gives a clear, debuggable flow suitable for a moderate number of services. For many small services, choreography might be a better fit.

---

## Final thought

Sagas are a pragmatic pattern: they trade immediate, global atomicity for availability and scalability. They force you to think about compensations, idempotency, and observability — disciplines that make distributed systems more robust in the real world.
keyTakeaways: Sagas break a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions plus compensations to achieve eventual consistency.
Choose orchestration for clear, central control and choreography for decoupled, event-driven systems.
Idempotency, observability, timeouts, and well‑designed compensations are essential to avoid long‑term inconsistencies.
